assessment.nobel_worthiness: Circuit QED opened a new regime of light-matter interaction on a chip: strong coupling of a superconducting artificial atom to a single microwave photon in a resonator, giving dispersive readout, coherent control and photon-mediated qubit coupling. It is the architecture behind essentially all superconducting quantum processors, and it is a clean, controlled demonstration of basic quantum phenomena, not just an engineering result. It also follows naturally from the recognition of macroscopic quantum tunnelling in circuits.
assessment.attribution: Blais, Girvin and Schoelkopf et al. (2004 theory) and Wallraff et al. (2004 experiment, Yale) are the decisive core. A three-person prize of Schoelkopf (experiment, Yale), Wallraff (first strong-coupling experiment and later ETH development) and Girvin (theory) is workable. Blais is the lead theory author and the exclusion is a real credit issue that the committee would have to weigh carefully. I am close to this field and would defer to colleagues on the fine allocation.
assessment.maturity: Strong coupling has been reproduced in many laboratories and the platform is mature and stable in interpretation. Timing is good, a little over two decades after the key papers, although the 2025 prize for the same broad platform means the committee must judge whether a second recognition so soon is warranted.
uncertainties: Whether Blais should displace one of the three proposed names.
Possible overlap with the 2025 prize for superconducting circuits, and my own proximity to this community.
Credit for the cQED idea relative to earlier cavity QED with atoms (Haroche, Walther, Kimble, already partly recognised).

assessment.nobel_worthiness: The Cirac-Zoller proposal (1995) for quantum gates with trapped ions and the subsequent experimental realisation of high-fidelity entangling gates, algorithms, error-correction primitives and analog/digital quantum simulation made ions the benchmark platform for quantum control. The step from a concrete theoretical proposal to a verified experimental quantum computing and simulation toolbox is a convincing example of foundational physics becoming an enabling platform.
assessment.attribution: Cirac and Zoller are the theoretical originators; Blatt led the Innsbruck experiments realising gates, entanglement and simulation at scale. This is a natural, compact configuration. Wineland (already a 2012 laureate) and others such as Monroe or Wineland-group contributions are outside the supplied names, and the credited list supports a fair three-way prize. Cirac and Zoller also appear under other candidates, which is an attribution overlap to note.
assessment.maturity: Experiments are independently reproduced across several groups and the physics is well understood. Recognition is timely, since both the foundational theory and the experimental realisation are decades old and the platform remains central.
uncertainties: Overlap in credit with optical-lattice quantum simulation and Rydberg arrays, where Cirac and Zoller also appear.
How much of the prize should recognise the 2012 Wineland work already honoured versus new contributions.
Whether quantum computing as such is still ahead of demonstration of fault tolerance.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: BB84 and the foundation of quantum cryptography showed that quantum mechanics itself can secure communication, turning no-cloning and measurement disturbance into a protocol. It is conceptually original and has been realised experimentally in many forms, and it connects to the 2022 prize for entanglement and Bell tests.
assessment.attribution: Bennett and Brassard are the unambiguous originators of BB84, which supports a two-person prize. Ekert's E91 protocol is an independent, entanglement-based proposal; the credited list contains two spellings of his name, and I would use neither since the clean credit is BB84. This leaves a real allocation question that the committee would need to discuss.
assessment.maturity: Theory is from the 1980s and practical systems and satellites have been demonstrated, although security of real devices with side channels is still an active issue. Recognition is arguably overdue and mature in concept.
uncertainties: Whether omitting Ekert (E91) is a fair resolution of credit.
Whether the discovery is physics enough or primarily information theory and cryptography.
Duplicate Ekert name entries in the credited list indicate inconsistent data.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: Cavity optomechanics brought macroscopic mechanical oscillators into the quantum regime: ground-state cooling, quantum-limited measurement, squeezing and entanglement of mechanical motion. It is a clear example of a new regime of physics opened by careful control of every physical detail, and it connects naturally to microwave circuit work such as electromechanics.
assessment.attribution: Aspelmeyer, Kippenberg and Painter led distinct, decisive experiments in optical and nanophotonic systems; Cleland led complementary quantum-ground-state work with superconducting qubit-coupled resonators. Selecting three of four credited names inevitably leaves out an important contributor, and the field is broad.
assessment.maturity: Quantum ground state and entanglement results have been reproduced across platforms. The applications (sensing, transduction) are still developing, so recognition is plausible but perhaps slightly early.
uncertainties: Exclusion of Cleland from a three-person prize.
Whether the discovery is one coherent advance or a collection of related milestones.
Contribution of earlier theory and early cooling work not captured in the supplied credit.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: Optical lattice clocks reached 10^-18 fractional uncertainty, enabling relativistic geodesy, tests of fundamental constants and a path to the redefinition of the second. The magic-wavelength lattice idea of Katori and the extreme precision realised by Ye are original and clear.
assessment.attribution: Katori proposed the magic-wavelength optical lattice clock and Ye led the record-precision realisation and many-body clock work. Two laureates is a clean configuration; the prize would build on earlier recognition of frequency combs (2005) and ion clocks (2012).
assessment.maturity: Multiple laboratories have reproduced and improved the clocks, so confirmation is strong. The practical redefinition of the second is still pending, but the science is mature.
uncertainties: Whether the community sees this as an increment on earlier precision-metrology prizes.
Contributions from other clock groups (ions, strontium and ytterbium teams) not in the credited list.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: Quantum error correction and fault tolerance establish that large quantum computations are possible in principle despite noise, and topological codes introduced a new way to protect information. Foundational and conceptually deep, and central to the future of the field I work in. Recent below-threshold experiments make it timely.
assessment.attribution: Shor (nine-qubit code, algorithm, fault tolerance), Steane (CSS-type codes) and Kitaev (toric code, topological protection) are the principal originators, though Calderbank, Gottesman, Knill, Laflamme and others also made decisive contributions that are outside the supplied names. This makes the configuration contestable.
assessment.maturity: Experimental confirmation of error suppression with increasing code size is only beginning. The theory is stable but full-scale fault tolerance is not yet demonstrated, which makes the prize arguably premature as a physics discovery.
uncertainties: Omission of other key code and threshold-theorem authors.
Whether it is a physics discovery or mathematical and computer-science theory.
Experimental validation is still early.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: Magic-angle twisted bilayer graphene opened a rich platform for flat-band correlated phases, unconventional superconductivity and later fractional states, and the Bistritzer-MacDonald theory predicted the magic angles. It is an outside-my-expertise area, so I defer to condensed-matter colleagues, but it clearly opened a new regime.
assessment.attribution: The theory (Bistritzer and MacDonald) and the 2018 experiments (Jarillo-Herrero group) are the decisive contributions, and the three names are a natural prize. Cao and others are not credited, and the roles of students and collaborators are a possible allocation issue.
assessment.maturity: Many groups have reproduced the correlated and superconducting phases, but the nature of the superconductivity and sample dependence are still debated, so the interpretation is not fully settled.
uncertainties: Sample variability and the unresolved pairing mechanism.
Credit relative to earlier moire and Dirac-fermion work, including the 2010 graphene prize.
Limited personal expertise outside quantum devices.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: Quantum simulation with ultracold atoms in optical lattices (the superfluid-Mott transition and later fermionic Hubbard physics, single-site imaging) provides a controlled way to study many-body models, and it gave a clear observation of a quantum phase transition in a tunable system.
assessment.attribution: Bloch, Greiner and Esslinger led the key experiments (Mott transition, quantum gas microscope, fermionic Hubbard), while Cirac and Zoller proposed the Bose-Hubbard realisation (Jaksch et al. is not in the credited names). Choosing among five names is difficult, and the theory proposal is a major credit question.
assessment.maturity: The work is reproduced widely, but the scientific payoff in answering open problems of strongly correlated matter is still developing, so the case is partly about promise.
uncertainties: Omission of Cirac and Zoller, whose proposal initiated the field.
Whether the achievement is a method rather than a discovery.
Overlap with the Bose-Einstein condensation recognition in 2001.
